title: Care Plan Review Procedure
summary: How and when we review each person's care plan and risk assessments with them: the 6-week review, scheduled reviews at least every 6 months, reviews triggered by a change, how reviews are prepared and held, how changes are approved and shared with care workers, commissioners and health professionals, and how overdue reviews are found and escalated. For managers, Care Coordinators, Field Care Supervisors and Senior Care Workers.

keyPoints.intro: This procedure tells you when a person's care plan must be reviewed, how to review it with them, and how to make sure every care worker knows what has changed before their next visit.
points: Every care plan and its risk assessments are reviewed with the person at a home visit within 6 weeks of care starting, then at least every 6 months, and sooner whenever their needs, wishes or circumstances change.

Record any change in the person in the daily visit notes and tell the office (On-call Manager out of hours) the same day, before you leave if it puts them at risk. If the care plan no longer matches the person, phone before acting.

If you are the Care Coordinator, decide the same working day whether a reported change, such as a hospital stay, a fall, new pressure damage, a medicines change or repeated refusals, needs a review, and record the review type and deadline in the care plan.
If the care plan can no longer be followed safely, have the affected parts updated and approved before the next visit. Never leave a known risk waiting for the scheduled review.

Before a review, read the records since the last review, including the daily visit notes, incident log, body maps, eMAR exceptions and visit times, and ask at least two of the person's core care workers what they have noticed.
Review with the person, not about them: ask whether their goals are being met and whether they are happy with their visits and care workers and, if they agree, ask them alone whether they feel safe.

At every full review, check every risk assessment, best interests decision and restriction, and end any restriction no longer needed. If you doubt the person can make a decision, follow the Mental Capacity Act and Best Interests Policy.

Update the care plan within 2 working days of the review. Never approve changes you wrote, and never use a change before it is approved, except an urgent out-of-hours safety change made by the On-call Manager.
Every care worker on the person's rota is told what has changed, by phone or message, the same day it is approved and always before their next visit, and who was told is recorded.
Tell the commissioner in writing within 2 working days when a review finds the person needs more, less or different support, and share changes with health professionals with the person's consent.
Reviews due and overdue are checked every week. An overdue review is held within 10 working days of its due date; one more than 1 month overdue is reported to the Nominated Individual.

blocks.p: A care plan is only safe while it is accurate. {{organisation}} reviews every person's care plan and risk assessments with them at set times and whenever something changes, judges each review by whether the person's own goals are being met rather than whether tasks were done, and makes sure every care worker works from the current, approved version. This procedure applies the review standard in the Person-Centred Care, Dignity and Respect Policy and the care plan rules in the Needs Assessment and Care Planning Policy.
This procedure sets when reviews happen, who decides that a change needs one, and how reviews are prepared, held, recorded, approved, shared and kept on time.

This procedure applies to every person we support, however their care is funded, to their whole care plan in CareFlow and every linked risk assessment and specialist plan, and to all staff who arrange, carry out, approve or contribute to reviews.

Writing the first care plan, short-notice starts and restarts are covered by the Needs Assessment and Care Planning Policy; the method for rating risk by the Risk Assessment and Home Environment Risk Assessment Procedure; medicines reviews by the Assessing Medicines Support Needs Procedure; and returns from hospital by the Hospital Admission and Discharge Procedure.

rows: Full review
A review of the whole care plan and every linked risk assessment with the person at a home visit. The 6-week review and every scheduled review are full reviews.
Focused review

A review of the parts of the care plan and risk assessments affected by a particular change, held at a home visit unless the reviewer records why a visit is not needed, for example where only visit times or contact details change.
Reviewer
A Field Care Supervisor or Care Coordinator authorised as an assessor under the Needs Assessment and Care Planning Policy, or the Deputy Manager or Registered Manager.
Completed
A review is completed when the revised care plan, or a confirmation that nothing has changed, is approved in CareFlow.
Overdue

A scheduled review not held by the next review date, a triggered review not held by its recorded deadline, or a review held but not approved within the timescales in Updating the care plan and records.

blocks.p: The Directors give reviewers the time, travel and staffing to hold reviews at home on time. The Nominated Individual challenges review performance at the Monthly Quality and Governance Meeting and takes the escalations in Finding and acting on overdue reviews.

The Registered Manager owns this procedure, authorises reviewers and approvers, approves the care plans reserved to managers, decides when a person declines recommended changes, and acts on overdue reviews. The Deputy Manager covers these duties in the Registered Manager's absence, audits completed reviews and produces the monthly review report.

Care Coordinators keep review dates, decide on reported changes, allocate and book reviews, carry out reviews when authorised, brief care workers, make the contacts this procedure sets and run the weekly check.

Field Care Supervisors carry out most reviews with their risk assessment reviews, observe changed tasks, replace the home copy of the care plan, and check at spot checks that care matches the current care plan.

Out of hours, the On-call Manager decides whether a reported change makes the care plan unsafe at the next visit, makes the urgent safety change the Needs Assessment and Care Planning Policy allows, briefs the care workers affected and hands over by 10am on the next working day.

subsections.heading: Senior Care Workers and Care Workers

blocks.p: Senior Care Workers and Care Workers record changes in the daily visit notes and tell the office (the On-call Manager out of hours) the same day, before leaving the home where the person is at risk, and call 999 in an emergency. Where the care plan no longer matches the person or their home, they phone a Senior Care Worker or the Care Coordinator (On-call Manager out of hours) before doing anything they are unsure of; they never change the care plan themselves. They give reviewers their views and check the care plan for changes at the start of every visit.

bullets: Regulation 9 requires us to assess the person's needs and preferences collaboratively with them, design care to meet them, and enable the person to make, or take part in making, decisions about their care to the maximum extent possible.

Regulation 12(2)(a) and (b) require us to assess the risks of the care we give and do all that is reasonably practicable to reduce them; Regulation 12(2)(i) requires timely care planning with others who share or take over the person's care.

Regulation 17(2) requires systems to monitor and improve quality and safety, to monitor and reduce risks, to keep an accurate, complete and contemporaneous record for each person, and to seek and act on feedback.

Under section 27 of the Care Act 2014 the local authority must keep its care and support plans under review generally, review a plan on a reasonable request by or on behalf of the person, and revise it where satisfied that circumstances have changed in a way that affects it.

Under section 1 of the Mental Capacity Act 2005 a person is assumed to have capacity unless it is established that they lack it, and anything done for a person who lacks capacity must be in their best interests and consider less restrictive options.
Providers of publicly arranged adult social care must have regard to the Accessible Information Standard (DAPB1605, version 1.1.0, published 3 July 2025).

blocks.p: The law does not set how often a provider must review a care plan. Our timescales are our policy, and we apply them and the Accessible Information Standard to everyone we support, including people who pay for their own care.

rows: 6-week review
Within 6 weeks of the first visit. The approver sets the date when the first care plan is approved. For a short-notice start, it is a separate visit from the full care plan visit within 7 days.
Full review at home, by the assessor who wrote the care plan wherever possible.
Ongoing scheduled review

At least every 6 months after the 6-week review. The reviewer sets a shorter interval of 1, 2 or 3 months where needs are changing quickly, and records why. A High residual risk is also reviewed at least every 3 months under the Risk Assessment and Home Environment Risk Assessment Procedure.
Full review at home.
Medicines support
6 weeks after medicines support starts, which is the 6-week review where it starts with the care, and at every full review.
Under the Assessing Medicines Support Needs Procedure, at the same visit wherever the dates allow.

blocks.p: A full review, whether scheduled or triggered, sets the next review date at 6 months, or the shorter interval set, from the date of that review. A focused review does not change it. A scheduled review falling due while the person is in hospital is held at the full review within 7 days of discharge; while care is paused for another reason, within 7 days of care restarting.
The following always trigger a review by the deadline shown.

rows: Return home from hospital
Full review at home within 7 days of discharge, however care restarted, under the Hospital Admission and Discharge Procedure.
A fall; new or worsening pressure damage; an injury, choking episode or other incident causing harm; a near miss showing the care plan is wrong
Focused review of the affected sections and risk assessments within 7 days, and before the next visit where the care workers' method is no longer safe.
Change in health, mobility, continence, swallowing, skin or cognition; new advice from a health professional; new equipment; a care worker reports the person needs more help than the care plan allows

Focused review within 7 days. New professional advice that changes how care is given, and new equipment, are written into the care plan, with care workers trained in the equipment, before the next visit at which they apply. Where more help is needed, the Care Coordinator reviews by phone with the care worker and the person the same day.
Reason to doubt the person's capacity for a decision about their care, or a change of attorney or deputy
Focused review within 7 days, with a capacity assessment under the Mental Capacity Act and Best Interests Policy; before the next visit where the decision has to be made at that visit.
Change in medicines, a medicines incident involving the person, or a pattern of declined doses
eMAR updated as the Medicines Management Policy requires; medicines support reviewed within 7 days under the Assessing Medicines Support Needs Procedure.
Change in a family carer's circumstances, or the person moves home

Full review within 7 days. The Care Coordinator updates the missed-visit contingency and risk level the same working day; where care a family carer gave stops suddenly, they arrange cover before it is next needed and tell the commissioner the same working day. A new home has its home environment risk assessment before the first visit there.
Safeguarding concern

Focused review of risks and the care plan within 7 days of the concern being raised, or sooner where the safeguarding lead decides, in line with any interim safety plan; reviewed again when the safeguarding plan is agreed or changes and when the record is closed.

The person declines all or most of the care at a visit at two consecutive visits or three times in seven days, or repeatedly cancels visits as the Visit Cancellations and Refusals of Care Procedure defines
Focused review within 7 days, with the person, under that procedure.
Two or more no-reply or no-access visits in 4 weeks, or the person going missing
Focused review within 7 days, including the no-reply plan, under the No Reply, No Access and Missing Person Procedure.
A missed visit that harmed the person, or two or more missed visits to the person in 4 weeks or a calendar month
Focused review of visit times, missed-visit risk level and staffing within 7 days of the second missed visit, or of the visit that caused harm.
The person may be approaching the last weeks of life

Full review within 2 working days of being told by a health professional, the person or their family. The Care Coordinator then checks with the person or family at least weekly whether the care plan still meets their needs, and holds a focused review whenever it does not.
Check-in and check-out show a visit 10 minutes or more longer or shorter than planned at 3 or more visits in 2 weeks, or visit time is used flexibly at 3 or more visits in a month
Focused review of visit length or tasks with the person within 7 days, asking the commissioner within 2 working days where they must agree a change.
A complaint, spot check or audit shows the care plan does not match the person's needs or wishes
Focused review within 7 days of the finding.
A request for a review from the person or their representative

Review within 10 working days of the request, or sooner where the request suggests a risk. A request for a specific change of times, tasks or care workers follows the timescales in the Person-Centred Care, Dignity and Respect Policy.
A request from the commissioner, or a change to the commissioned hours or tasks
By the commissioner's deadline, or within 10 working days; the care plan is always updated and approved before the change takes effect.

subsections.heading: Deciding whether a change needs a review

steps: Office staff record every reported change in the person's daily visit notes the same working day and pass it to the Care Coordinator; out of hours the On-call Manager receives it.

The Care Coordinator decides the same working day whether the change is a trigger in the table above, whether the care plan can still be followed safely at the next visit, and whether a full or focused review is needed.

Where the care plan cannot be followed safely at the next visit, the Care Coordinator updates the affected parts and has them approved before that visit; out of hours the On-call Manager makes the urgent safety change, which the Registered Manager or Deputy Manager checks by the end of the next working day.
The Care Coordinator records the trigger, the decision, the type of review and its deadline in the care plan, and allocates a reviewer.
Where the Care Coordinator decides that no review is needed, they record why. The same change reported again within 4 weeks always leads to a review.

The Care Coordinator books every scheduled review at least 2 weeks before its due date, at a time that suits the person and anyone they want present, and books triggered reviews as soon as the deadline is set.

At least 5 working days before a scheduled review (by phone when a triggered review is booked), the Care Coordinator tells the person, in the format recorded in their care plan, when it is, who is coming, that it usually takes 45 to 60 minutes and the questions they will be asked, and invites anyone the person wants to join them. Professional interpreters are booked as the Communication and Accessible Information Policy sets out.

The reviewer reads, since the last review: the care plan and risk assessments; the daily visit notes (in full for the last 4 weeks, for themes before that); incident log entries and body maps; safeguarding records; eMAR exceptions and declined doses; check-in and check-out records for visit times and lengths; the person's continuity rate; complaints and feedback; and spot check and quality check results.
The reviewer asks at least two members of the person's core care team (all of them if fewer) what has changed, what works and what does not, and records their views.
The reviewer gathers letters and advice from health professionals, the hospital and the local authority, and, with the person's consent, invites the professionals involved to contribute or attend.

The reviewer checks for an attorney, deputy, advocate, open capacity question, restriction or open safeguarding plan, so that the right people are invited, and for any recorded risk to staff at the address, taking a second member of staff where the Lone Working and Staff Personal Safety Policy requires one.

blocks.p: The review is a conversation with the person at their pace, using their communication aids, starting with what they want to talk about. Family, carers and advocates take part as the person wishes. If the person agrees, the reviewer spends time alone with them, with a professional interpreter where one is needed and never a family member, to ask how they are treated and whether they feel safe; anything suggesting abuse or neglect is reported under the Safeguarding Concerns: Reporting, Referral and Enquiry Procedure. Where a task has changed, such as a transfer or a skin check, the reviewer joins a care visit to watch it being done, with the person's agreement, before rewriting it. The review itself never takes time from a care visit.

columns: What the reviewer checks with the person
rows: Goals and what matters to me
Whether each goal is met, partly met or not met, in the person's words and against its measure of success; what they want to keep, stop or change.
Experience of care
Whether visit times suit them; how care workers treat them; their continuity rate; anything they want to praise or complain about.
Needs, support and visit plans
What the person now does themselves and whether each instruction is still accurate; visit times, lengths, care worker numbers and essential tasks against check-in and check-out records.
Risks and restrictions

Every risk assessment, under the Risk Assessment and Home Environment Risk Assessment Procedure; whether each control still works and is the least restrictive; whether each restriction is still needed, ending any that is not; positive risk-taking plans under the Positive Risk-Taking Policy.
Medicines
The medicines support review under the Assessing Medicines Support Needs Procedure.
Communication
Communication and information needs, and whether they are recorded, flagged and met as the Accessible Information Standard requires.
Consent, capacity and authority

Consent to care; capacity assessments and best interests decisions; any new lasting power of attorney, deputyship or advance decision; any sign that care amounts to a deprivation of liberty, which the Registered Manager acts on under the Deprivation of Liberty in the Community Procedure.
People involved

Who they want involved and what may be shared with whom; what family carers and other agencies visiting do, such as medicines or meals; how family carers are coping and whether they have been offered a carer's assessment; whether an independent advocate is needed.
Access, absence and emergencies

Missed-visit risk level and contingency; no-reply plan; key safe or key arrangements, offering a routine key safe code change at least every 12 months (codes are never written in the care plan); what goes to hospital with the person and who looks after their home.
Health, future wishes and home

Professionals' advice; the surprise question under the End of Life Care Policy; any advance care plan, DNACPR decision or ReSPECT form and where it is kept; the home environment risk assessment; equipment and its next examination date; telecare.

blocks.p: A focused review covers the affected areas and always includes the person's views, consent and the related risk assessments.

subsections.heading: When the person lacks capacity or declines

blocks.p: Where the person lacks capacity for a decision about their care, the reviewer still involves them as fully as possible and consults their attorney or deputy (within that authority), family, carers and advocates under the Mental Capacity Act and Best Interests Policy.

A person who does not want a review is offered another date, a shorter visit, a review by phone or a review with someone they trust present. If they still decline, the reviewer completes the review from the records and the care team's views, records the person's wishes, and tells the Registered Manager. Where a person with capacity declines changes the reviewer recommends, the Registered Manager decides within 1 working day whether care can continue safely and tells the commissioner in writing, as the Needs Assessment and Care Planning Policy sets out. Where a declined change leaves a significant risk to staff, the Health and Safety Policy steps for a declined control measure also apply.

sections.heading: Updating the care plan and records

steps: The reviewer records the review in the care plan on the day of the visit, under their own log-in: the date, type of review and trigger, how it was held, who took part, the person's views in their own words, the outcome for each goal, decisions made and why, and actions, each with an owner and deadline.

Within 2 working days of the review the reviewer updates the care plan and risk assessments in CareFlow, or records that nothing has changed, and records the person's agreement with the date, how it was given and who was present, or why it could not be given.

An approver who did not write the changes approves them within 2 working days of submission, and before the next visit for anything affecting safety. Approvals the Needs Assessment and Care Planning Policy reserves to managers apply to every review.
The approver confirms the next review date in the care plan. Earlier versions of the care plan and risk assessments stay in CareFlow and are never deleted.

Within 5 working days of the review, the Care Coordinator sends the person a short written summary of what was agreed and what will change, in their preferred format, and the Field Care Supervisor replaces the copy of the care plan in the home and returns the old copy to the office for secure destruction.

rows: Every care worker on the person's rota
What has changed and what they must now do differently.
By the Care Coordinator, by phone or message, the same day the change is approved and always before their next visit, recording who was told; out of hours by the On-call Manager.
The person and their chosen representative
Any change affecting their safety; the review summary.
The same day for safety changes; the summary within 5 working days.
The commissioner
Needs that have increased, reduced or changed, goals not being met, or a change needed to hours, times, tasks or medicines support.

In writing by the Care Coordinator within 2 working days of the review; by the Registered Manager, by email, the same day where a care worker reports the person needs more help than the care plan allows. A change in scope is agreed before it takes effect. For a person who pays for their own care, any change to visits or charges is agreed with them in writing first.
Health professionals involved
Changes relevant to their care, and any concern needing their assessment.

With the person's consent, or as the Confidentiality and Information Sharing Policy allows, within 2 working days; the same day where urgent. Medicines changes as the Medicines Management Policy requires.

blocks.p: Where the person would be at risk before the commissioner agrees extra support, the Registered Manager, or the On-call Manager out of hours, may authorise it as an interim arrangement, recording why in the care plan, and the Registered Manager confirms or ends it with the commissioner within 5 working days.

sections.heading: Reviews led by the local authority or NHS

blocks.p: When a local authority or NHS continuing healthcare team reviews its own plan, the Care Coordinator sends a written summary of the person's needs, progress towards their goals and changes we recommend by their deadline or within 5 working days of the request, and a reviewer attends where invited and the person agrees. Our care plan is then reviewed with the person and approved before any change takes effect. Where our review finds needs have changed and the local authority arranges the care, the Care Coordinator tells the person that they, or someone for them, may ask it to review its plan.

sections.heading: Finding and acting on overdue reviews

blocks.p: CareFlow flags care plans whose review is due within 30 days (the default setting, which we keep) or overdue. Every week the Care Coordinator checks unbooked reviews due in the next 30 days, overdue scheduled and triggered reviews, and revised care plans awaiting approval, and acts as follows.

rows: Any review overdue
Reason recorded in the care plan; review held within 10 working days of the due date; listed at the weekly management meeting.
Care Coordinator
Overdue by more than 2 weeks
Registered Manager confirms with the care team that the current care plan is still safe to follow, and allocates another reviewer or carries out the review within 5 working days.
Registered Manager
Overdue by more than 1 month, or more than 5% of reviews overdue

Reported to the Nominated Individual within 2 working days of being found, and to the Monthly Quality and Governance Meeting with a recovery date, as the Governance and Quality Assurance Policy requires.
Registered Manager to the Nominated Individual
Overdue by more than 3 months
Reported to the Directors and added to the risk register until resolved.
Nominated Individual
A visit given after a 'before the next visit' deadline was missed
Recorded in the incident log the same day and reviewed by the Registered Manager or Deputy Manager by the end of the next working day.
Care Coordinator

blocks.p: Reviews, decisions not to review, agreement, approvals and review dates are kept in the care plan; risk reviews in the risk assessments; medicines changes in the eMAR. Retention follows the Records Management and Retention Policy.

blocks.p: Each reviewer's annual observed assessment under the Needs Assessment and Care Planning Policy includes observing a review, recorded in supervision and appraisal records. A reviewer whose review an audit finds has a significant error, such as a missed risk or a change used before approval, is given feedback within 5 working days and completes two further supervised reviews before reviewing alone again.

blocks.p: Every shortfall is recorded with an action, an owner and a deadline in the service improvement plan and tracked to completion.

This procedure is reviewed every 12 months by the Registered Manager, checked by the Nominated Individual and approved by the Directors under the Policy Management and Document Control Policy. It is reviewed sooner after a change in law or national guidance, a serious incident, an inspection finding, or when monitoring shows our arrangements are not working.
